unit.title: Quantities, Variables, and Mathematical Objects
unit.act: Act I - Giving general names to quantities
unit.role: Establish what algebra describes before asking students to manipulate it.
unit.governingQuestion: How can symbols name quantities and relationships without erasing their meaning?
unit.storyArc: Concrete quantities become tables, graphs, verbal rules, expressions, equations, and inequalities. Students learn what kind of object each notation represents and how substitution preserves structure.
outcomes: Identify changing, fixed, unknown, and parameter quantities.
Translate among verbal, numerical, graphical, and symbolic representations.
Parse terms, factors, coefficients, and grouping structure.
Substitute and evaluate while preserving units and parentheses.
unit.investigation: Model equipment rental cost using a context, table, graph preview, expression, and equation.
unit.mastery: Students classify mathematical objects, translate representations, and evaluate formulas with signed inputs and units.

lessons.title: Variables and changing quantities
lessons.outcome: Distinguish unknowns, changing quantities, parameters, constants, and labels.

opening.prompt: Track altitude over time and decide which quantities vary.
opening.purpose: Name each quantity’s role before using symbols so variables, unknowns, parameters, constants, and labels are not confused.

prerequisiteChecks: Identify what changes in a distance-over-time table.
Distinguish a number from a unit label.
Describe the horizontal and vertical quantities on a simple graph.
exposition: A variable is a symbol assigned to a quantity, not merely a letter waiting to be solved. Its role comes from context. In h(t), time t varies and altitude h depends on it. A letter can instead represent one unknown value, a fixed parameter controlling a family, or a label with no numerical role.

A constant keeps the same value within the model. A parameter is held fixed during one instance but may change between instances. In C = mt + b, t may vary, C depends on t, and m and b act as parameters selecting one cost plan.

Good algebra begins with a quantity dictionary: symbol, meaning, units, allowed values, and role. This prevents meaningless substitutions and makes graphs, tables, and formulas describe the same relationship.

definitions.definition: A quantity allowed to take more than one value in the situation.
definitions.conditions: Its allowable values form its domain.

definitions.definition: A fixed but not yet determined value satisfying stated conditions.
definitions.conditions: An unknown is not necessarily changing.

definitions.definition: A value held fixed in one model but varied to compare a family of models.
definitions.conditions: State what the parameter controls.

examples.prompt: In h = 1200 − 80t, identify each quantity and role.
steps: Read h as altitude in feet and t as elapsed time in seconds.
t varies and h depends on t.
1200 and −80 are constants describing initial altitude and rate.
examples.answer: t: independent variable; h: dependent variable; 1200 and −80: constants
examples.interpretation: Symbols gain meaning from the quantity dictionary.

examples.prompt: In y = mx + b, explain why m is often a parameter.
steps: Hold m fixed to draw one line.
Change m to select a different line.
Observe that x still varies along each chosen line.
examples.interpretation: A parameter indexes a family while variables move within one member.

examples.prompt: A box marked A contains 12 bolts. Is A a variable?
steps: Ask whether A is assigned a numerical quantity.
Here A only names the box.
The bolt count 12 is the numerical constant.
examples.interpretation: Not every letter in a mathematical display is a variable.

lessons.title: Expressions, equations, and inequalities
lessons.outcome: Classify symbolic objects by whether they name a value or make a true-or-false claim.

opening.purpose: Classify expressions, equations, and inequalities so the goal of the work is clear before any manipulation.

prerequisiteChecks: Compare 9 and 12 using an order symbol.
exposition: An expression names a value but does not make a claim, so 3x + 2 has no truth value by itself. An equation claims two expressions are equal. An inequality claims one expression is ordered relative to another.

Evaluation finds an expression’s value for supplied inputs. Solving finds all inputs that make an equation or inequality true. Simplifying rewrites an expression without changing its value on its domain. These are different goals and require different conclusions.
The equal sign means 'has the same value as,' not 'the answer comes next.' Reading a chain such as 2(5)+1 = 10+1 = 11 is valid because every expression in the chain has the same value.

definitions.definition: A mathematical object that names a value.
definitions.conditions: It has no true-or-false status by itself.

definitions.definition: A statement that two expressions have equal value.
definitions.conditions: Its solution set contains inputs making the statement true.

definitions.definition: A statement comparing the order of two expressions.
definitions.conditions: Its solution set often contains an interval of values.

steps: = makes an equation; < makes an inequality.
examples.interpretation: Classification identifies whether to evaluate, solve, or compare.
Evaluation returns a value, not a solution set.
The resulting true statement 5 = 5 verifies the solution.

lessons.title: Terms, factors, coefficients, and structure
lessons.outcome: Read nested sums and products without flattening them incorrectly.

opening.prompt: Dissect a formula with several layers of grouping.
opening.purpose: Read sums, products, coefficients, and nested grouping from the outside in without flattening structure.

exposition: Terms are the addends of a sum, while factors are the multiplicative pieces of a product. In 3x + 5, the terms are 3x and 5; inside the first term, 3 and x are factors. A coefficient is the numerical factor multiplying a variable expression.

Structure is nested. In 2(x + 4) − 3, the outermost operation is subtraction, while multiplication and addition occur inside its parts. Reading the expression tree from the outside inward prevents illegal combinations.
A fraction bar groups the entire numerator and denominator. In (x+1)/(x−2), neither plus nor minus is an outermost operation; the whole numerator is divided by the whole denominator.

definitions.definition: An addend in a sum after subtraction is interpreted as adding an opposite.
definitions.conditions: Terms are identified at the current grouping level.

definitions.definition: A multiplicative component of a product.
definitions.conditions: Factors can themselves be grouped sums or quotients.

definitions.definition: A numerical factor multiplying a variable or variable expression.
definitions.conditions: The implied coefficient of x is 1 and of −x is −1.

steps: Read subtraction as addition of opposites.
examples.interpretation: Terms are separated only at the outer sum level.

steps: The outer operation is multiplication by 5.
The second factor is a square.
The squared base is the grouped difference x − 2.
examples.answer: Product of 5 and the square of x−2
examples.interpretation: The description preserves nested structure.

examples.prompt: Find the numerator and denominator of (2x+1)/(3−x).

lessons.title: Substitution and evaluation
lessons.outcome: Replace variables or subexpressions with equal-valued expressions while preserving grouping.

opening.prompt: Evaluate a cost formula for several signed and fractional inputs.
opening.purpose: Substitute equal values or expressions while protecting grouping, signs, and units.

prerequisiteChecks: Explain why parentheses can preserve a negative input.
exposition: Substitution replaces a symbol or subexpression with an equal-valued quantity. The replacement must occupy the same structural position as the original symbol, so parentheses are essential around negative numbers, fractions, and multi-term expressions.
Evaluation is substitution followed by arithmetic. A clear evaluation line first shows the replacement, then simplifies in justified steps. Units should travel with measured quantities.
Substitution may also replace one expression with an equivalent expression. If y = 2x + 1, then 3y − 4 becomes 3(2x+1) − 4. The parentheses preserve y as one complete object throughout the rewrite.

definitions.definition: Replacement of a symbol or subexpression by an equal-valued quantity.
definitions.conditions: The replacement must retain the original grouping role.

definitions.definition: Find the numerical value of an expression for specified inputs.
definitions.conditions: Show the substitution before arithmetic.

definitions.definition: The complete expression inserted for a symbol.
definitions.conditions: Use parentheses when it contains more than one term or a leading sign.

examples.interpretation: Parentheses ensure the negative input is squared.

examples.prompt: If y = 2x + 1, rewrite 3y − 4 in terms of x.

opening.prompt: Resolve two calculator entries that appear similar but mean different things.
opening.purpose: Use grouping and precedence to read expressions unambiguously and enter them correctly in calculators.

exposition: Order of operations is a reading convention for expressions without extra grouping. Grouping symbols override the default order and communicate which expression is one unit. Exponents apply to their complete bases before multiplication and addition.

Multiplication and division share one precedence level and are processed left to right; addition and subtraction do the same. The mnemonic PEMDAS becomes misleading if it suggests multiplication always precedes division.

Calculator syntax must preserve written grouping. A fraction such as (x+1)/(x−2) needs parentheses around both numerator and denominator when typed on one line. Spacing alone does not create a mathematical group.

definitions.conditions: The entire grouped expression is evaluated together.

definitions.definition: A typed expression that can be read in more than one way.
definitions.conditions: Add parentheses rather than relying on visual spacing.

lessons.title: Properties of real-number operations
lessons.outcome: Use commutative, associative, identity, inverse, and distributive properties to justify rewrites.

opening.prompt: Rearrange a calculation to make it easier without changing its value.
opening.purpose: Use properties of real-number operations to justify efficient, equivalent rewrites.

prerequisiteChecks: Use an area model to explain 3(4+2).
exposition: Properties describe transformations that preserve value. Commutative properties change order, associative properties change grouping, identities leave a value unchanged, and inverses combine to an identity.
The distributive property links multiplication with addition: a(b+c)=ab+ac. It works in both directions, enabling expansion and factoring. Distribution applies to every term in the grouped sum.

A written solution should name the property that licenses each non-arithmetic rewrite. This turns symbolic movement into a proof of equivalence rather than a pattern guess that happens to look familiar.

definitions.definition: Order may be reversed in addition or multiplication.
definitions.conditions: Subtraction and division are not commutative.

definitions.definition: Grouping may change in repeated addition or multiplication.
definitions.conditions: It does not change the order of terms or factors.

definitions.definition: Multiplication by a sum equals the sum of the products.
definitions.conditions: Every term inside the group receives the outside factor.

steps: Use commutativity to place 25 and 4 together.
examples.interpretation: The properties change order and grouping without changing value.
The sign of the outside factor applies to both products.

steps: Rewrite each term as a product containing 6.
examples.interpretation: Factoring exposes the common multiplicative structure.

lessons.title: Equivalent expressions and like terms
lessons.outcome: Recognize rewrites that preserve value for every allowed input and combine only structurally alike terms.

opening.prompt: Compare two formulas by testing and then proving equivalence.
opening.purpose: Recognize equivalent expressions and combine only terms with identical variable structure.

prerequisiteChecks: Explain why 3 apples + 2 apples can combine.
exposition: Equivalent expressions have the same value for every allowed input. Numerical testing can disprove equivalence but cannot prove it for all inputs; properties provide a general proof across the full domain.

Like terms have identical variable factors raised to identical powers. Their coefficients count copies of that shared unit, so 3x+5x=8x. Terms x and x² are not alike, just as meters and square meters are not alike.

A reliable simplification sequence distributes first, identifies terms with signs attached, groups like structures, and combines coefficients. The result should be checked at one convenient input to catch arithmetic errors.

definitions.definition: Expressions equal for every input in their common domain.
definitions.conditions: A proof uses properties or a complete algebraic derivation.

definitions.definition: Terms with exactly the same variable part, including exponents.
definitions.conditions: Only their numerical coefficients may differ.

definitions.definition: A term with no variable factor.
definitions.conditions: It is like only other constant terms.

examples.interpretation: The variable structure x is preserved.
Distribution reveals the like terms.

lessons.title: Formulas, units, and mathematical communication
lessons.outcome: Read formulas as reusable relationships and communicate transformations unambiguously.

opening.prompt: Use an area, distance, or finance formula with units.
opening.purpose: Read formulas as relationships among measured quantities and write substitutions and transformations so another reader can verify them.

prerequisiteChecks: State units for length and area.
Solve a one-step multiplication fact such as 4x=20.
exposition: A formula is a reusable relationship among quantities. Every symbol should be declared with meaning and units. Dimensional consistency constrains sensible substitutions and catches many transcription errors.

Using a formula requires more than inserting numbers: identify the target quantity, select the correct relationship, substitute with grouping and units, compute, and interpret the result. A numerical answer without a unit or context is incomplete when the inputs are measured.
Rearranging a formula isolates a chosen quantity while preserving equality. The same equation may be useful in several solved forms, but restrictions such as nonzero divisors must be recorded.

definitions.definition: An equation expressing a reusable relationship among quantities.
definitions.conditions: Every symbol and unit should be declared.

definitions.definition: An equation containing several letters representing quantities.
definitions.conditions: It may be rearranged to solve for one chosen quantity.

definitions.definition: Matching dimensions across equal or added quantities.
definitions.conditions: It is a necessary check on a measurement formula.
